Ancient Israel and Judah were two Israelite kingdoms that existed in the Southern Levant during the Iron Age.
This Greek god of medicine, said to be a son of Apollo, had daughters named for concepts like Health and Recuperation, and represents the healing side of the ancient medical arts — who is he?
Asclepius (Ancient) is a hero and god of medicine in ancient Greek religion and mythology.

Baudouin of Belgium (7 September 1930 - 31 July 1993) was King of the Belgians from 17 July 1951 until his death in 1993.
A mechanic and trade unionist from León radicalized by state repression, he became a celebrated anarchist militant and martyr of the Spanish Civil War — who was he?
Buenaventura Durruti (14 July 1896 - 20 November 1936) was a Spanish anarcho-syndicalist militant and a leading figure in Spanish anarchism before and during the Spanish Civil War.

Chlothar II (May/June 584 - 18 October 629) was king of the Franks, ruling Neustria (584-629), Burgundy (613-629) and Austrasia (613-623).
Taking office at just 35, this Ecuadorian businessman-turned-politician became the second-youngest president in his country's history. Who is he?
Daniel Noboa (born 30 November 1987) is an Ecuadorian politician and businessman serving as the 48th and current president of Ecuador since 2023.

Earl Warren (March 19, 1891 - July 9, 1974) was an American attorney and politician who served as the 30th governor of California from 1943 to 1953, and as the 14th chief justice of the United States from 1953 to 1969.

Installed in 1933 and developed by António de Oliveira Salazar, this corporatist authoritarian regime evolved from a 1926 military coup against Portugal's unstable First Republic. What regime is this?
Estado Novo (Portugal) (lit. 'New State') was the corporatist Portuguese state installed in 1933.
A pivotal figure in the 1918-1919 German Revolution, this Social Democratic Party leader became his country's first president, serving from 1919 until his death in 1925 — who was he?
Friedrich Ebert (4 February 1871 - 28 February 1925) was a German politician of the Social Democratic Party (SPD) who served as the first president of Germany from 1919 until his death in 1925.
Founded in 918, this Korean kingdom achieved what historians call the peninsula's first true national unification, ruling until the Joseon dynasty was established in 1392 — what kingdom was it?

Goryeo (Middle) was a Korean state founded in 918, during a time of national division called the Later Three Kingdoms period, that unified and ruled the Korean Peninsula until the establishment of Joseon in 1392.

Islam Karimov (30 January 1938 - 2 September 2016) was an Uzbek politician who served as the first president of Uzbekistan, from the country's independence in 1991 until his death in 2016.

A Democratic attorney and Army National Guard officer who served in Kandahar Province, this North Carolina official became the state's 52nd attorney general in 2025 after previously representing its 14th congressional district — who is he?
Jeff Jackson (politician) (born September 12, 1982) is an American politician, attorney, and Army National Guard officer who has served as the 52nd attorney general of North Carolina since 2025.
His pivotal role in Hong Kong's 2014 Umbrella Movement landed this teen activist on Time's Most Influential Teens list and a Person of the Year nomination — who is he?
Joshua Wong (Cantonese; born 13 October 1996) is a Hong Kong activist and politician.

Emerging from the breakup of the Western Turkic Khaganate in the late 6th century CE, this semi-nomadic Turkic people built a powerful trading empire spanning parts of modern Russia, Ukraine, and Kazakhstan — who were they?

Khazars (/kzrz/) were a semi-nomadic Turkic people who established a major commercial empire in the late 6th century CE spanning the south of modern European Russia, southern Ukraine, and western Kazakhstan.

An army doctor who earned the Medal of Honor on the frontier, he commanded the Rough Riders with Theodore Roosevelt as his deputy and later became a leading contender for the 1920 presidential nomination. Who was he?
Leonard Wood (October 9, 1860 - August 7, 1927) was a United States Army major general, physician, and public official.

Serving non-consecutive terms from 1981 to 2003 and again from 2018 to 2020, this Malaysian physician-turned-politician is his country's longest-serving prime minister, with a political career spanning 75 years — who is he?
Mahathir Mohamad (born 10 July 1925) is a Malaysian politician, physician and author who served as the fourth and seventh prime minister of Malaysia from 1981 to 2003 and again from 2018 to 2020.
After seizing power in a coup, this leader ran Benin under a Marxist-Leninist banner for 18 years, lost office, then returned via the ballot box in 1996. Who was he?

Mathieu Kérékou (French; 2 September 1933 - 14 October 2015) was a Beninese politician who served as president of the People's Republic of Benin from 1972 to 1991 and the Republic of Benin from 1996 to 2006.
A Lango politician, this man served as Uganda's first prime minister after independence in 1962, governing in coalition with President Mutesa II before a bitter rift split them. Who is he?

Milton Obote (28 December 1925 - 10 October 2005) was a Ugandan politician who served as the Prime Minister of Uganda from 1962 to 1966 and the president of Uganda from 1966 to 1971 and later from 1980 to 1985.
Whose members were nicknamed 'Nazbols,' this Russian opposition organization was banned as extremist in 2007 and published a newspaper named after a hand grenade — which group?
National Bolshevik Party was a Russian political party that operated from 1993 until it was banned in 2007.
This KGB bureau chief in London spied for British intelligence from 1974 until his dramatic 1985 exfiltration, after which Moscow sentenced him to death in absentia — who is he?
Oleg Gordievsky (assumed name: Anton Kelsen; 10 October 1938 - 4 March 2025) was a colonel of the KGB who became KGB resident-designate (rezident) and bureau chief in London and a British spy.

Losing a 2022 Conservative leadership contest to Liz Truss before briefly serving as Leader of the House of Commons, this British politician lost her own Portsmouth North seat to Labour in 2024 — who is she?
Penny Mordaunt (born 4 March 1973) is a British former politician who served as Lord President of the Council and Leader of the House of Commons from 2022 until 2024.
Emerging from a so-called 'Chekist takeover' of state and economic assets, this term describes the political system built around one Russian leader's inner circle — what is it?
Putinism is the social, political, and economic system of Russia formed during the political leadership of Vladimir Putin.
This French lawyer and politician, serving as Minister of Justice under François Mitterrand, enacted the abolition of the death penalty in France in 1981 — who is he?

Robert Badinter (French; 30 March 1928 - 9 February 2024) was a French lawyer, politician, and author who enacted the abolition of capital punishment in France in 1981, while serving as Minister of Justice under Franois Mitterrand.
A native of Zanzibar, she became the first woman to lead her country when she ascended from the vice-presidency after John Magufuli's death in 2021 — which Tanzanian president is she?
Samia Suluhu Hassan (soo-; born 27 January 1960) is a Tanzanian politician and the sixth president of Tanzania, serving since 19 March 2021.
This Indian politician has served two separate terms as Chief Minister of Karnataka, and was only the second person ever to complete a full five-year term in that office — who is he?

Siddaramaiah (born 3 August 1947), also referred to by his nickname Siddu, is an Indian politician, lawyer, former lecturer and statesman who served as the 16th Chief Minister of Karnataka from 2013 to 2018 and 2023 to 2026.
Before becoming French prime minister in 2025, this Renaissance party politician held ministerial posts covering local authorities, overseas territories, and the armed forces — who is he?
Sébastien Lecornu (French; born 11 June 1986) is a French politician who has served as Prime Minister of France since September 2025.

Claudius: Roman emperor from AD 41 to 54.

Dacia: Ancient kingdom in Southeastern Europe (168 BC – 106 AD)

Gwangju Uprising: 1980 anti-government protest in South Korea.

Hayato Ikeda: Prime Minister of Japan from 1960 to 1964.

Himyar: Former kingdom in ancient Yemen. Himyar was a polity in the southern highlands of Yemen, as well as the name of the region which it claimed.

Jezebel: Biblical figure; Phoenician princess and wife of Ahab.

Khosrow II: Emperor of the Sasanian Empire from 590 to 628.

Li Qiang: Premier of China since 2023.

Manu (Hinduism): Hindu concept. Manu (Sanskrit: मनु) is a term found with various meanings in Hinduism.
Honored in Gnostic texts as the 'apostle to the apostles,' this follower of Jesus witnessed both his crucifixion and resurrection — who was she?
Mary Magdalene: Saint and follower of Jesus. Mary Magdalene is regarded by believers as a historical figure, possibly from Magdala.
The longest-serving governor in Massachusetts history, this Democrat lost the 1988 presidential election to George H. W. Bush — who is he?

Known simply as MBZ, this Sandhurst graduate and former Air Force pilot became the third president of the UAE and ruler of Abu Dhabi in 2022 — who is it?
Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan: President of the United Arab Emirates since 2022.

Picts: Medieval tribal confederation in northern Britain.

Known as 'The Destroyer' within the Hindu trinity alongside Brahma and Vishnu, this deity is the Supreme Lord who creates, protects, and transforms the universe in one major tradition. Who is this god?
Shiva: Major deity in Hinduism. Shiva is one of the five equivalent deities in Panchayatana puja of the Smarta tradition of Hinduism.

Syriza: Political party in Greece. It was founded in 2004 as a political coalition of left-wing and radical left parties, and registered as a political party in 2012.
Known as 'the Great,' this Roman emperor was the last to rule the entire empire single-handedly and helped enshrine the Nicene Creed as orthodox doctrine — who was he?
Theodosius I: Roman emperor from 379 to 395.

Yoon Suk Yeol: President of South Korea from 2022 to 2025.

Calouste Gulbenkian (born 1869) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Maria Goeppert Mayer (born 1906) is the earliest of the four. In 1986, the Maria Goeppert Mayer Award for early-career women physicists was established in her honor.
Which of these four was founded earliest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
MUMPS (founded 1966) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Samuel C. C. Ting is a physicist.
Pick the chemist from these four.
What is the atomic number of Lawrencium?
Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lr (formerly Lw) and atomic number 103.
In what year was Dolph Lundgren born?
Dolph Lundgren: Hans "Dolph" Lundgren (Swedish: [ˈdɔlːf ˈlɵ̌nːdɡreːn]; born 3 November 1957) is a Swedish-American actor, filmmaker, and martial artist.
In what year was Molybdenum discovered?
Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.
In what year was Titanium discovered?
Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
Mikoyan MiG-27: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. It is based on the Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-23 fighter aircraft, but optimised for air-to-ground attack.
In which country is Dassault Rafale based?
Dassault Rafale: France. Dassault built a technology demonstrator that first flew in July 1986 as part of an eight-year flight-test programme, paving the way for approval of the project.
Who is credited with discovering Technetium?
Technetium: Emilio G. Segrè. Technetium is a chemical element; it has symbol Tc and atomic number 43.
Who is credited with discovering Cell theory?
Who is credited with discovering Hydrazine?
Hydrazine: Hermann Emil Fischer. Hydrazine is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula N2H4.
Sharing the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physics for unifying the weak and electromagnetic forces, who became the first Muslim scientist to win a Nobel?
Abdus Salam (29 January 1926 - 21 November 1996) was a Pakistani theoretical physicist and Nobel laureate.
Which diverse group of aquatic photosynthetic organisms excludes land plants but includes seaweeds that can grow up to 50 metres long?
Algae (UK also; sing.: alga) are any of a large and diverse group of photosynthetic organisms.

This American anthropologist specialized in the economic anthropology and rural development of Indonesia, earning her PhD from the University of Hawaii in 1992 after studying women's weaving and blacksmithing on Java. Who was she?
Ann Dunham (November 29, 1942 - November 7, 1995) was an American anthropologist who specialized in the economic anthropology and rural development of Indonesia.
This medical condition, most often caused in the developed world by liver cirrhosis, is the abnormal buildup of fluid within the abdominal cavity — what is it called?
Ascites is the abnormal build-up of fluid in the abdomen.
This self-taught Maryland-born mathematician published a successful series of almanacs and assisted Major Andrew Ellicott in surveying the new federal capital district — who was he?
Benjamin Banneker (November 9, 1731 - October 19, 1806) was an American naturalist, mathematician, astronomer and almanac author.
What hydrated mineral salt of sodium, mined economically in only a few places worldwide, forms a white crystalline solid that can be dehydrated by heating?
Borax (also referred to as sodium borate, tincal and tincar) is a salt (ionic compound) normally encountered as a hydrated borate of sodium, with the chemical formula Na2H20B4O17.

Native to the Philippines and nearby Southeast Asia, this small sour citrus fruit — a natural hybrid of kumquat and mandarin — flavors everything from marinades to beverages in Filipino cooking — which fruit?
Calamansi (Citrus microcarpa), also known as calamondin, Philippine lime, or Philippine lemon, is a citrus hybrid cultivated predominantly in the Philippines.
Separated from the small intestine by the ileocecal valve, this pouch — whose Latin root means 'blind' — kicks off the large intestine and, in herbivores, helps ferment cellulose. What is it?
Cecum (plural ceca or) is a pouch within the peritoneum that is considered to be the beginning of the large intestine.
This roughly 24-hour internal biological cycle, generated within an organism but tuned by cues like daylight, is regulated by an internal biological clock — what is it called?
Circadian rhythm is a natural oscillation that repeats roughly every 24 hours.
Entering service with Strategic Air Command in 1960, this four-engine, delta-wing supersonic bomber was the first in the world capable of Mach 2 — name the aircraft?

Convair B-58 Hustler is a supersonic strategic bomber, the first capable of Mach 2 flight. To achieve the high speeds desired, Convair chose a delta wing design used by contemporary interceptors such as the Convair F-102.

He's the only person to have won BAFTAs in black-and-white, colour, high-definition, 3D and 4K — a broadcasting career that began way back in 1954 hosting Zoo Quest. Who is this English natural historian?
David Attenborough (born 8 May 1926) is an English broadcaster, natural historian, and writer.
What flying insect, of which about 3,000 species exist, is known for its large compound eyes, two pairs of transparent wings, and often iridescent, metallic body coloration?
Dragonfly is a flying insect belonging to the infraorder Anisoptera below the order Odonata.
Tissue similar to the uterine lining grows elsewhere in the body—often on the ovaries, fallopian tubes, or pelvis—affecting roughly 10% of women of reproductive age worldwide. What is this condition?
Endometriosis is a disease in which tissue similar to the endometrium - the lining of the uterus (womb) - grows elsewhere in the body.
Every member of this mammal family is an obligate carnivore with retractile claws and a powerful bite, from forest dwellers to desert hunters — which family is it?
Felidae is the family of mammals in the order Carnivora colloquially referred to as cats.
This Austrian-school economist shared the 1974 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Gunnar Myrdal for work on how prices communicate information — who is he?
Friedrich Hayek (8 May 1899 - 23 March 1992) was an Austrian economist and philosopher.
This ancient metabolic pathway breaks glucose down into pyruvate through ten enzyme-catalyzed reactions in a cell's cytosol, generating ATP along the way. What process is it?
Glycolysis is the metabolic pathway that converts glucose (C6H12O6) into pyruvate and, in most organisms, occurs in the liquid part of cells (the cytosol).
This wingless insect spends its entire life on the human scalp, feeds only on blood, and has legs too short and stumpy to jump or even walk well on a flat surface — what is it?
Head louse (Pediculus humanus capitis) is an obligate ectoparasite of humans.
Native to Japan, this deciduous shrub grows big flower heads that can turn pink or blue and is also known as the mophead or lacecap — which plant?
Hydrangea macrophylla is a species of flowering plant in the family Hydrangeaceae, native and endemic to Japan.
Lasting anywhere from a few days to over a month, this disorder makes it hard to fall or stay asleep, leaving daytime drowsiness, irritability and trouble focusing in its wake — what is it?
Insomnia is a sleep disorder causing difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep for as long as desired.
This psychologist edited 'Psychological Review' from 1910 to 1915 and was later ranked the 17th most-cited psychologist of the 20th century for popularizing behaviorism — who is he?
John B. Watson (January 9, 1878 - September 25, 1958) was an American psychologist who popularized the scientific theory of behaviorism, establishing it as a psychological school.
Named after the American endocrinologist who identified it in the 1940s, this chromosome anomaly, also called 47,XXY, typically affects phenotypic males with infertility. What condition is it?
Klinefelter syndrome (KS), also known as 47,XXY, is a chromosome anomaly.

Equal to about 9.46 trillion kilometres, this astronomical distance unit is defined by how far illumination travels through a vacuum in 365.25 days — despite its name, it isn't a measure of time. What is it?
Light-year (ly or lyr), is a unit of length used to express astronomical distances and is equal to exactly 9460730472580.8 km, which is approximately 9.46 trillion kilometres or 5.88 trillion miles.
Which Australian nut-producing tree genus, an important bushfood for Aboriginal peoples, was first commercially cultivated at scale not in its native country but in Hawaii?
Macadamia is a genus of four species of trees in the flowering plant family Proteaceae.
This cone-shaped structure at the base of the brainstem controls involuntary functions from heart rate and breathing to vomiting and sneezing — what is it called?
Medulla oblongata is a long stem-like structure which makes up the lower part of the brainstem.
Some of these tiny eight-legged arachnids live in soil as decomposers, others on plants causing galls, and one destructive parasite targets honeybee colonies — what are they?
Mite are small arachnids (eight-legged arthropods) of two large orders, the Acariformes and the Parasitiformes, which were historically grouped together in the subclass Acari.
This leafy Brassica rapa crop, native to the area around Beijing, became a widespread vegetable across Europe, the Americas, and Australia in the 1900s — which vegetable?
Napa cabbage (Brassica rapa subsp. In much of the world, it is referred to as "Chinese cabbage".
Also called the coypu, this plant-eating rodent digs streamside burrows and now troubles several countries as an invasive species far from its South American home — what is it?
Nutria (Myocastor coypus) is an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent from South America.

Covered in large protective keratin scales, these mammals — sometimes called scaly anteaters — range across Asia and sub-Saharan Africa and are the only mammal order known to have such scales — what are they?
Pangolin are mammals of the order Pholidota. The one extant family, the Manidae, has three genera: Manis, Phataginus, and Smutsia.
A self-described socialist active in Finland's Pirate Party, this entrepreneur co-founded a famous file-sharing search engine and later started the privacy service Njalla — who is he?
Peter Sunde (born 13 September 1978), alias brokep, is a Swedish-born Finnish-Norwegian entrepreneur and politician.
Emerging roughly 203 million years ago and wiped out alongside the dinosaurs 66 million years ago, this order of long-necked marine reptiles ruled Jurassic seas — what were they?
Plesiosaur are an order or clade of extinct Mesozoic marine reptiles, belonging to the Sauropterygia.
Unfolding inside every cell in two acts called transcription and translation, this process turns a gene's DNA into messenger RNA on its way to building enzymes and hormones — what is it?
Protein biosynthesis is a core biological process, occurring inside cells, balancing the loss of cellular proteins (via degradation or export) through the production of fresh proteins.
Belonging to the genus Ribes and native to western Europe, which berry carries the scientific name Ribes rubrum and has spread into the wild in many regions?
Redcurrant (Ribes rubrum) is a member of the genus Ribes in the family Grossulariaceae.
Sitting in group 4 just below hafnium, this synthetic element named for a famous physicist has a most-stable isotope that survives only about 48 minutes — which element is it?
Rutherfordium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rf and atomic number 104.
Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, this term describes an unplanned fortunate discovery, as with penicillin or the microwave oven — what is it called?
Serendipity is an unplanned fortunate discovery. The concept is often associated with scientific and technological breakthroughs, where accidental discoveries led to new insights or inventions.

Born in the Bronx to Puerto Rican parents and raised by her mother after her father's death, this Princeton grad became the third woman on the U.S. Supreme Court after Barack Obama's 2009 appointment — name this justice?
Sonia Sotomayor (born June 25, 1954) is an American lawyer and jurist who serves as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States.
This small nocturnal marsupial sails between trees on membranes stretched from wrist to ankle, and its Latin name translates as 'short-headed rope-dancer' — what animal is it?
Sugar glider (Petaurus breviceps) is a small, omnivorous, arboreal, and nocturnal gliding possum.

This mass of gray matter forming part of the forebrain relays sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex through radiating nerve fibers, and helps regulate consciousness, sleep, and alertness — what's the structure?
Thalamus (pl.: thalami; from Greek, "chamber") is a large mass of gray matter on the lateral wall of the third ventricle forming the dorsal part of the diencephalon (a division of the forebrain).
Not a single branch of the family of life but a strategy evolved over and over — a tall trunk and branches reaching for sunlight — describes which kind of perennial plant?
Tree is a perennial plant with an elongated stem, or trunk, usually supporting branches and leaves.

This flowering plant genus, the largest in its family with over 680 species, is found mostly across the temperate Northern Hemisphere but also as far-flung as Hawaii and the Andes. What is this plant commonly called?
Viola (plant) is a genus of flowering plants in the family Violaceae.
Passed only from fathers to sons, this genetic structure carries the SRY gene that typically triggers development of male gonads in mammals — what is it?
Y chromosome is one of two sex chromosomes in therian mammals and other organisms.
Genetic in roughly 80% of cases, this long-term skin condition clogs hair follicles with dead skin and sebum, producing blackheads and pimples on the face, chest, and back — what is it?
Acne: Skin condition characterized by pimples.

German-born theoretical physicist celebrated for E=mc² and work on relativity — he won the 1921 Nobel Prize not for those breakthroughs, but for discovering the photoelectric effect. Who revolutionized physics across multiple domains?
Commonly called buffalo, this large grazing mammal endemic to North America is one of just two living species in its genus, alongside a European cousin — what animal is it?
American bison: Species of bovid artiodactyl mammal.

Characterized by extreme food restriction and a fear of gaining weight despite being underweight, this eating disorder is described in the DSM-5 as involving a disturbance in how one perceives their own body shape — what's the condition called?
Anorexia nervosa: Eating disorder. Individuals with anorexia nervosa have a fear of gaining weight, despite the fact that they are typically underweight.
Caused by excessive exposure to silver dust or compounds, this condition turns the skin a striking blue or blue-gray shade, especially in sun-exposed areas — what's it called?
Argyria: Medical condition. The most dramatic symptom of argyria is that the skin turns blue or blue-gray, and is usually most prominent in sun-exposed areas of the skin.
Native to the Americas and prized for thousands of years for its unusually oily fruit, this evergreen of the laurel family bears what's botanically a giant berry around a single seed — what is it?
Avocado: Species of flowering plant in the laurel family.

When no one else had the staff for it, this American lawyer volunteered to prosecute the Einsatzgruppen trial at Nuremberg, then spent decades championing an International Criminal Court — who was he?
This small, fluid-filled pocket that forms in the skin's upper layers — usually from friction, burns, or infection — gets the name 'bleb' when it's especially tiny. What is it?
Blister: Small pocket of fluid within the upper layers of the skin. The word "blister" entered English in the 14th century.
Typically about two-thirds copper and one-third zinc, which prehistoric substitutional alloy differs from bronze, which swaps in tin instead of zinc?
Brass: Alloy of copper and zinc. Brass has long been popular for its bright, golden appearance and is used for drawer pulls and doorknobs.
The world's most widely consumed psychoactive substance works by mimicking adenosine's shape and blocking its receptors, keeping you awake — what is this stimulant?

This German-Swedish pharmacist had a knack for discovery — molybdenum, tungsten, barium, chlorine, and arguably oxygen all trace to his bench — but the same hands-on chemistry may have killed him via mercury poisoning. Which unlucky genius is it?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele: Swedish German chemist who discovered oxygen (1742–1786)
Descended from land mammals but now fully aquatic, this group swims via up-and-down tail strokes and includes toothed members capable of echolocation — what group includes whales and dolphins?
With about 3,400 species in over 520 genera, this insect family includes nearly every member of its group except two species in a small sister taxon — which family?
Used to treat gout, familial Mediterranean fever, and pericarditis, this medication has such a narrow therapeutic index that its injectable form was pulled from the US market in 2008. What is it?
Colchicine: Medication mainly used to treat gout. The American College of Rheumatology recommends colchicine, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or steroids in the treatment of gout.
Produced mainly by the adrenal cortex and surging in response to stress and low blood sugar, this steroid hormone is sold as medicine under the name hydrocortisone — what is it?
Built from microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules, this network gives a cell its shape and lets it contract and migrate — what is it?
Cytoskeleton: Network of filamentous proteins that forms the internal framework of cells.
Carnations and sweet williams both belong to which flowering plant genus of about 340 species, native mainly to Europe and Asia?
Attracted to rotting fruit and fermenting drinks, this insect became the first animal launched into space in 1946 and has earned six Nobel Prizes for scientists who studied it — what is it?
Drosophila melanogaster: Species of fruit fly.
The first woman to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, this political scientist earned it in 2009 for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons — who was she?
This term covers a range of spiritual traditions built around hidden or occult knowledge, appearing in Christian, Buddhist, Hindu, and Quranic contexts alike — what is it?
Esotericism: Topics referred to by the same term.
First confirmedly detected in 1992 orbiting a pulsar, this term describes any planet found outside our solar system — what is it?
Exoplanet: Planet outside of the Solar System. The first confirmed detection of an exoplanet was in 1992 around a pulsar, and the first detection around a main-sequence star was in 1995.
From the Latin word for 'tube' or 'pipe,' this medical term describes an abnormal connection between two hollow spaces in the body — what is it?
Fistula: Abnormal connection between two hollow bodily spaces, often organs.

Unlike plants, this kingdom of life can't photosynthesize, and unlike most things, it has chitin in its cell walls — feeding instead by oozing digestive enzymes out and absorbing what dissolves. What group includes yeasts, molds, and mushrooms?
Fungus: Organism belonging to kingdom Fungi.
Endemic to China and sporting a handy 'thumb' on its forepaw to grip bamboo, this black-and-white bear weighs in around 100 to 115 kg — what animal is it?
Giant panda: Species of bear. The giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca), also known as the panda bear or simply panda, is a bear species endemic to China.
Sporting pied black-and-white plumage with a red patch on its lower belly, this Palearctic bird drums on trees to mark territory and excavate nest holes — which species?
Great spotted woodpecker: Species of bird. The great spotted woodpecker (Dendrocopos major) is a medium-sized woodpecker with pied black and white plumage and a red patch on the lower belly.
Caused by mutations in the ABCA12 gene, this severe genetic skin disorder covers newborns in thick, cracked plates resembling armor — what is it?
Harlequin-type ichthyosis: Genetic skin disease. Harlequin-type ichthyosis is a genetic disorder that results in thickened skin over nearly the entire body at birth.

Bred by Polynesians in the pre-Columbian era from two Pacific island species, this tropical flowering plant is the national flower of Malaysia and the unofficial national flower of Haiti — what is it?
Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis: Hybrid species of flowering plant. It is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant in the tropics and subtropics.
Carl Wilhelm Scheele pinned down this gas's composition in 1777; it's flammable, smells of rotten eggs, and kills by blocking cellular respiration much like cyanide — what colorless compound is it?
Hydrogen sulfide: Poisonous and flammable gas. Hydrogen sulfide (preferred IUPAC name and American English) or hydrogen sulphide (Commonwealth English) is a chemical compound with the formula H2S.
Patented in 1961 and used to fight fever, pain and inflammation by blocking the cyclooxygenase enzyme, this drug sits on the WHO's List of Essential Medicines — what is it?
Before he proposed that the Earth behaves like one self-regulating living system, this English independent scientist built the detector that first revealed CFCs lurking in our atmosphere. Who was he?
A former Navy SEAL turned physician, this NASA astronaut flew to the International Space Station in 2025 as part of Expedition 72/73 after earning a Silver Star for valor in combat — who is he?
Jonny Kim: American astronaut, physician, and former U.S. Navy SEAL (born 1984)
This Gram-negative rod bacterium can turn deadly if aspirated into the lungs, producing a telltale bloody, brownish-yellow jelly-like sputum — which pathogen?
Klebsiella pneumoniae: Species of bacterium. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a Gram-negative, non-motile, encapsulated, lactose-fermenting, facultative anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium.
Its lens-shaped seeds, usually two to a pod, are split and simmered into the dal that's a staple across the Indian subcontinent — which legume?
Lentil: Species of plant with edible seeds.
This four-engine American turboprop can land on dirt strips and unprepared runways, then moonlight as a gunship, a flying firefighter, or a weather scout — which versatile workhorse is it?
Lockheed C-130 Hercules: American military transport aircraft.

With a fruiting body resembling an open umbrella, this fungus often grows in fairy rings across Eurasian pastures and is prized as a good edible despite resembling toxic look-alikes — what's its scientific name?
Macrolepiota procera: Species of fungus. Macrolepiota procera, the parasol mushroom, is a basidiomycete fungus with a large, prominent fruiting body resembling a parasol.
A Zainichi Korean entrepreneur, this founder and CEO of SoftBank turned a $20 million bet on Alibaba in 2000 into a stake worth around $75 billion — who is he?
Developed in 1955 and later sold under the brand name Dianabol, this anabolic steroid was once widely used for physique and performance enhancement — what is it?
Metandienone: Androgen and anabolic steroid. It is also used non-medically for physique- and performance-enhancing purposes.
Normally equal to 60 seconds, which unit of time has occasionally run 61 seconds long in UTC due to leap seconds, though a 59-second version has never actually occurred?
Minute: Unit of time equal to 60 seconds. The prime symbol ′ is also sometimes used informally to denote minutes.
Sold under the brand name Bactroban, this topical antibiotic treats impetigo and clears MRSA from the nose — what is it?
Derived from the Greek word for kidney, this medical specialty covers kidney function, disease, and treatments ranging from diet changes to dialysis and transplantation — which field?
Nephrology: Medical study concerned with the kidneys.
The largest structure inside a eukaryotic cell's nucleus, this site of ribosome assembly also helps form signal recognition particles and responds to cellular stress — what is it?
Nucleolus: Largest structure in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. The nucleolus also participates in the formation of signal recognition particles and plays a role in the cell's response to stress.

This vertebrate clade has skeletons made mostly of bone rather than cartilage, and includes both classic 'bony fish' and, cladistically, every land vertebrate descended from lobe-finned ancestors — what is it?
Osteichthyes: Diverse clade of vertebrate animals.
Named from the Latin word for 'sparrow,' this bird order — making up over half of all species — is defined by perching feet with three toes forward and one back. What's it called?
Passerine: Perching birds of the order Passeriformes.
Synthesized in 1938 by German chemist Otto Eisleb and later marketed as Demerol, this synthetic opioid was the go-to pain medication for much of the 20th century — what is it?
Pethidine: Opioid analgesic. Pethidine, also known as meperidine and sold under the brand name Demerol among others, is a fully synthetic opioid pain medication of the phenylpiperidine class.

Often stereotyped as ferocious predators, these South American freshwater fish actually have varied diets that include plant matter, making them more omnivorous than their reputation suggests. What fish are they?
Piranha: Common name for certain fishes of the family Serrasalmidae.
Chickens, turkeys, ducks, and geese all fall under this term for birds domesticated for meat, eggs, or feathers — what is it called?
Poultry: Domesticated birds kept by humans for their eggs, meat or feathers.

Described as 'the translation of politics into the reality that citizens experience every day,' this field implements government policies and programs to solve social and economic problems — what is it called?
Public administration: Academic discipline; implementation or management of policy.
Native to the southern United States, this pond terrapin is the world's most commonly traded and most invasive turtle, largely due to pet releases — which species?
This American neuroscientist and primatologist, a Stanford professor across three departments, has spent his career studying the neuroendocrinology of stress — who is he?
The largest genus in the mint family, this group of nearly 1,000 shrubs and herbs includes common cooking sage and rosemary — what's the genus called?
Salvia: Largest genus of plants in the mint family. Salvia is the largest genus of plants in the sage family Lamiaceae, with just under 1,000 species of shrubs, herbaceous perennials, and annuals.
Ejaculated through the urethra and containing fructose plus enzymes that help sperm survive their journey to fertilize an egg, this bodily fluid is also collected for animal breeding. What is it?
Semen: Reproductive biofluid of male or hermaphroditic animals.
This altered state cycles between REM and non-REM modes, and despite outward stillness it still produces active brain patterns — more reactive than a coma. What is it?
Sleep: Naturally recurring resting state of mind and body.

Synthesized by Aristotle and taken as fact for two millennia, this superseded theory held that maggots could arise straight from dead flesh, until Louis Pasteur helped discredit it — what was it called?
Spontaneous generation: Theory of life arising from non-living matter.
Born from Russia's PAK FA programme begun in 1999 and carrying the internal name T-50, this twin-engine jet was the first Russian military aircraft built with stealth technology — what is it?
Sukhoi Su-57: Russian stealth multirole fighter aircraft.
From Greek for 'arrangement' and 'method', this science names and classifies organisms into ranked groups — domain, kingdom, phylum, and on down to species — what is the field?

Taxonomy (biology): Science of classifying organisms. The principal ranks in modern use are domain, kingdom, phylum (division is sometimes used in botany in place of phylum), class, order, family, genus, and species.
What is the medical term for a clump of platelets, fibrin, and blood cells that forms within the circulatory system — sometimes lifesaving, sometimes an obstruction?
Thrombus: Blood clot. There are two components to a thrombus: aggregated platelets and red blood cells that form a plug, and a mesh of cross-linked fibrin protein.
Also known as all-trans retinoic acid, this medication treats acne as a topical cream but must be taken orally for leukemia patients with a specific gene fusion — what is it?
Tretinoin: Medication. Tretinoin, also known as all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), is a medication used for the treatment of acne and acute promyelocytic leukemia.
Known as the Great Bear, this constellation contains the seven-star pattern nicknamed the Big Dipper — what's it called?
Ursa Major: Constellation in the northern sky.
Sporting prominent tusks and whiskers, this Arctic pinniped's Pacific males can weigh over 2,000 kilograms, making it second in size among pinnipeds only to the elephant seals — what animal?
Walrus: Species of marine mammal with tusks.
Sold under the veterinary brand name Rompun and often combined with ketamine for animal sedation, which structural analog of clonidine is this alpha2-adrenergic drug?
Xylazine: Veterinary anesthetic, sedative and analgesic.
Lutetium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for lutetium is Lu. Lutetium is a chemical element; it has symbol Lu and atomic number 71.
Titanium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for titanium is Ti. Titanium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ti and atomic number 22.
